subsubtopic: INVESTIGATION INTO SAFETY OF DISPOSABLE BUTANE LIGHTERS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. I sincerely hope that all members will agree with my non-partisan motion as it affects the safety of millions of consumers.
In view of the fact that a number of people in North America have already lost their lives as a result of explosions of disposable butane cigarette lighters, which are said to have the same amount of force as approximately three sticks of dynamite, and because as recently as last night another similar accident critically injured comedian Richard Pryor who as of this moment is fighting for his life, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott):
That this House instruct the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to launch an immediate investigation into the safety of all disposable butane cigarette lighters in order to determine which brands should be removed from the marketplace and what appropriate safety warnings must be established.

speechtext:

The indexing of personal income tax to some extent prevents the tax man from profiting by inflation. This principle was first enunciated by the Hon. Robert Stanfield and adopted by the Hon. John Turner in his budget of 1974 as being an

June 10, 1980
element of fairness in the tax system. 1, therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a motion which I hope will gain the unanimous consent of the House.
Whereas the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) has confirmed that the previous Conservative government had approved plans to introduce a 35-cent stamp to commemorate the Moscow games this year, and whereas this government and many others have combined to boycott the Moscow games as a result of the U.S.S.R.'s invasion of Afghanistan, and whereas any action or gesture that might detract from the boycott's objective should not be pursued, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith):
That this House recommend to the Postmaster General that all and any plans to issue a stamp to commemorate the Moscow games be immediately terminated.

subsubtopic: INVESTIGATION INTO COSTS OF METRIC CONVERSION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing national necessity regarding false and misleading practices of the Metric Commission in implementing conversion to the metric standard of weights and measures.
The Canadian Metric Commission has advised municipal fire departments that conversion to metric can be accomplished at a cost of $5 per pumper-the cost of applying decals to the vehicle. In fact, according to fire officials the cost can run to as much as $13,000 per pumper, including hoses and connections but not taking into account the cost of changing fire hydrants.
In view of information provided by the Metric Commission being inaccurate and grossly misleading, and the actual costs to municipal fire departments being prohibitive in many cases, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer):
That a moratorium on the implementation of the metric conversion program be declared until the true costs are established and answers given as to whether metric conversion will result in better fire and rescue service, and will save more lives and more property, and whether or not litres of water will flow faster through metric hose.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. As we have seen today, the unemployment figures are again discouraging: there has been an increase to 7.8 per cent in the seasonally adjusted figure, which is worse than a year ago and worse than a month ago.
The minister, on April 21, predicted an average unemployment rate of 8 per cent this year. Back in December, the Department of Finance predicted a rate of 8.3 per cent. Since then, on May 27 the deputy minister of finance, in his evidence before a senate committee, predicted "a higher and more sustained increase in the unemployment rate than was projected last fall" and also, he went on to say, "the prolongation of rather severe unemployment rates."
Can the minister tell the House what average unemployment rate he predicts during this year and next year, and would he indicate, whether by a budget or in other ways, how he intends to deal with the increasing and serious economic problems in this country? If not by a budget, how does he intend to indicate his way of dealing with these problems?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member for St. John's West has pointed out, the projection for unemployment that I presented on April 21 was about 8 per cent, a somewhat different figure than had been presented by himself in the preceding December.
I have had no reason to change that projection for 1980. Perhaps it ought to be changed and will have to be changed

June 10, 1980
Oral Questions
with ongoing developments. 1 believe that the projections made by my hon. friend in December had to be changed as a result of new developments, and that may occur in this case; but at the present time I am not projecting an additional increase.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on April 24 the Prime Minister said, "Our main preoccupation is to ensure economic growth and jobs for Canadians and the deficit is a long-term objective." The firm of Wood Gundy has predicted, for the first time since 1954, that we are going to have a real decline in output in the Canadian economy-a decline of 0.5 per cent-which does not say much for economic growth. We know from the figures that jobs for Canadians are seriously in danger.
Could the minister tell the House how he plans to ensure economic growth and jobs for Canadians, especially in view of the present record high deficit that he is prophesying for this year in his budget and the high deficit in the balance of international payments? How is the minister going to carry out the Prime Minister's objective in the light of this situation?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
I should add, Madam Speaker, that the projection made by Wood Gundy is more pessimistic for growth in 1980 than the projection which 1 gave on April 21, which was real growth of one-half of 1 per cent. 1 notice that the president of the Royal Bank today gave a similar forecast. There is no doubt that as a result of declines in the United States and the absorption of very large oil price increases in the world economy, we are in a period of slow growth in Canada.
The hon. member has asked what my plans are with respect to dealing with that situation. I have said to my hon. friend that it is certainly not my intention at the moment to attempt to deal with that situation by recommending further increases in the very large fiscal deficit. I do not believe my hon. friend would recommend that course, either. There is a good deal of stimulus being provided by the very large deficit that is in existence at the present time. In the absence of that deficit, probably the unemployment rate-no question of probability, there is no doubt that the unemployment rate would be higher than it is at the present time.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is no question about it; the minister in office is a changed man from the minister out of office, and he had better get his act together.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Those on our left are only happy when there is trouble in the country.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
My final supplementary to the Minister of Finance is this. In the minister's speech in Paris recently, June 4, to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, he said:
To the extent that these changes include further reductions in the demand for oil-
Sorry, the minister said this:
But the experience of the 1970s has brought home the point that we are unlikely to achieve a sustained improvement in employment unless we get inflation under better control.
Does this indicate it will be the minister's policy direction and chief priority to introduce policies to get inflation under better control? Not policies directed at increasing employment but, rather, that the emphasis is going to be in getting inflation under better control? In other words, does he mean what he says, or does he not mean what he says, or does what he says mean anything?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, that convoluted series of questions would require an answer that only the hon. member would be capable of giving.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, there is always the dilemma of trying to deal with rising unemployment and the threat of inflation. The consensus of opinion at the OECD meeting of ministers of finance from the western industrialized countries was that at the present time it would be desirable to maintain the battle against inflation-not to attempt to reflate at the present time against the danger of renewed inflationary expectations.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Did you agree?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO DEAL WITH ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, I agreed with that approach. This is a situation that will have to be assessed as time goes on, particularly in view of what happens in other countries. But it would seem to be unwise today to begin to launch an abrupt change in policy and to assume that the threat to the economies of not only Canada but other countries from inflation is over. That would not be very wise.

subsubtopic: EXPENDITURES FOR JOB-CREATION PROGRAMS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. On April 21, the finance minister increased federal expenditures by $2 billion. In view of the rapidly increasing unemployment situation, can the minister tell the House how much of that $2 billion increase has been allocated for employment-creation projects?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: EXPENDITURES FOR JOB-CREATION PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member well knows- because he has been in the House and participated in debates-we have announced two job-creation programs, one a summer job-creation program which was in the neighbourhood of $100 million, and the program announced last Monday of $137 million. Those are direct job-creation programs.
June 10, 1980

1 would also remind the hon. member that in the last three months this government has brought forward a number of decisions that will stimulate the economy-the fighter aircraft decision, major investments in DREE programs, major investments to support Chrysler-all of which are deisgned to provide a stimulus for jobs across Canada in terms of longterm economic development. If you add all those up, we are probably investing in this country to the extent that our fiscal limits will allow.

subsubtopic: EXPENDITURES FOR JOB-CREATION PROGRAMS
speechtext:
There appears to be a contradiction between that statement and the statement of the Minister of Finance. If the Minister of Employment and Immigration is suggesting that $237 million out of the $2 billion is allocated toward job creation, I do not think we shall find it in the figures which were presented to us.
The labour force data released today suggests that in the past month this country has lost 68,000 jobs, on a seasonally adjusted basis; that is, 3,400 jobs lost each working day. Can the minister tell us whether, in his view, that loss is temporary or long-term and likely to accelerate?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: EXPENDITURES FOR JOB-CREATION PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can tell the hon. member that the contradiction is surely in the eyes of the beholder. In this case there is no difference whatsoever between myself and the Minister of Finance. What the Minister of Finance has just said is that we, like most economies, are influenced by a number of factors.
Certainly, there is the international factor-the softening in the U.S. market and the severe recession which the U.S. economy is now experiencing. So in terms of giving an answer, it depends partly on decisions made elsewhere, outside the borders of this country. But I can assure the hon. member that we will do everything we can to soften the impact and respond with a great deal of care and concern.

subsubtopic: HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT-PROGRAMS TO ALLEVIATE
speechtext:
I have a question for the Minister of Finance. The unemployment figures released today show that over 900,000 people are unemployed. The seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment is up in every region. Also, in the heartland of the Canadian manufacturing industry, Ontario, unemployment is up sharply, to a large extent because 30,000 auto workers and workers in related industries such as rubber, plastics and glass are unemployed and are not likely to resume employment, if ever, until 1981 or 1982.
Given these facts, can the minister tell us whether the government is considering new programs which will put a large proportion of our unacceptably high number of unemployed to work? Or are we to assume that the government has decided
Oral Questions
that these people will just have to live as best they can until the international economic situation improves?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT-PROGRAMS TO ALLEVIATE
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, I think that would be an unduly pessimistic attitude to take. The hon. member referred to the particular position of the auto industry. It seems to me that general demand policies would not have very much of an effect on improving the sales of automobile manufacturers. It is the kind of program announced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, namely, to permit companies like Chrysler to adjust to market conditions, which has the best chance of providing employment opportunities. That is the type of program we ought to be seeking in the present situation.

subsubtopic: HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT-PROGRAMS TO ALLEVIATE
speechtext: It seems to me highly unlikely that 900,000 unemployed are going to be in the market for cars, refrigerators, houses or anything else. Despite all the speeches about helping women to get jobs, or better jobs, figures today indicate that 400,000 women are looking for work. That is virtually 40 per cent of the work force. Does the government have any plans to ensure that more women will be able to find jobs in the coming year?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT-PROGRAMS TO ALLEVIATE
speechtext:
I think I should clarify my earlier answer to the hon. member so that he would realize that when I talked about the automobile industry, I had in mind those persons in that industry who are suffering from unemployment and whose only hope for future employment comes, not from general demand policies, but from structural readjustment within the industry itself so that the market opportunities for the product would be better.
As the hon. member knows, there are certain automobile manufacturers abroad who are competing very vigorously in the North American market because they have products which consumers want. That is the point I had in mind with respect to these unemployed.

subsubtopic: HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT-PROGRAMS TO ALLEVIATE
speechtext:
What about the second part?

Madam Speaker, to say the least, I am dismayed at what I consider to be a very cold and callous reply from the Minister of Finance, who himself comes from an area which has a large number of unemployed, to a very serious problem.
I would like to ask the minister a very specific question. Almost 50 per cent of the unemployed are young people under 24, and of those more than 400,000, 95,000 are students who are looking for work for the summer. They not only have difficulty finding jobs, but also in the calculations which the provinces make with respect to student aid it is assumed that 45 per cent of their needs will be met by income they earn

June 10, 1980

from working. Can the minister indicate what programs the government has to ensure that these people can find enough work so that they can go back to school this fall?

speechtext:

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING OF FIRST MINISTERS TO DISCUSS
subsubtopic: RENEWAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, three weeks to the day after the Quebec referendum, I have the pleasure to report to this House on yesterday's meeting of first ministers on the renewal of the constitution. My remarks will be brief because I do not want to impose upon hon. members' good will on this opposition day and also because the leaders of opposition parties, as well as private members, will undoubtedly want to ask me further questions on this subject. I would rather use the time allocated to me to answer specific questions.

June 10, 1980
Constitutional Renewal
The first thing to point out following yesterday's meeting is that it resulted in a collective decision which could prove most beneficial for Canada. In effect, all first ministers have committed themselves to reach by September major decisions on the constitution, and in order to do so they have given themselves a very tight three-month schedule of meetings and negotiations.
In fact, Madam Speaker, we have made a commitment, in our own name and in the name of our ministers and officials, to spend during the next three months twice as much time on the constitutional problem as was spent in the last two years by the federal and provincial governments combined.
This is evidence of the importance and urgency that both myself and the premiers attach to the renewal of the Canadian federalism and of our constitution. It is also a sign of our strong will to fulfil the promise we have made to Canadians to bring real and substantial improvements to the fundamental law of this country.
| English]
The hope of the federal government was that the premiers would want to join with us in urgent and effective action to give Canada a new constitution which will be fully responsive to the present and future needs of the country and its people. That hope has now grown into a joint federal-provincial commitment.
I, therefore, want to pay tribute to the premiers' open-mindedness and generosity of spirit which made that commitment possible. I realize we could not have made that commitment if we were not aware of the strong support for real reform among the people we represent, so I gladly pay tribute also to the spirit and the will of the people of Canada at this decisive moment in our history.

In that event, the federal government would have to give very serious consideration to its options and recommend to Parliament a plan of action which would allow us to fulfil our responsibilities to the people of Canada.

speechtext:
I am confident that the agreement we seek will both strengthen the rights and freedoms of the people and define a division of federal and provincial powers which will enable Canada to achieve its great potential. I am determined that, in our progress toward agreement, we will not engage in any trading-off of the rights and freedoms of the people against the powers of governments.
With the consent of the House, Madam Speaker, I will table the documents I distributed to the premiers yesterday. They are a meeting agenda, a statement of principles for a new constitution, a list of priority issues, and a calendar of meetings for first ministers and ministers between June 17 and September 12.
With regard to the priority issues, Madam Speaker, I would not want to mislead the House in any way. The copies which I have tabled and the copies which were distributed are a statement by the federal government. The list itself has been amended by adding one item to the list which we brought to the meeting yesterday, the item of fisheries. The only other difference between the list now tabled and the list that we circulated at yesterday's meeting is that our list yesterday had two columns; one column lists items that are of general interest to the people of Canada and the other column lists items concerning the division of powers between governments.
I commend to the earnest attention of all hon. members the two documents dealing with principles and priorities. It would be my hope that members from every part of Canada, and of all parties, would consider and discuss the contents of these papers among themselves and with their constituents.
Such consideration and discussion would not only assist the federal and provincial governments and Parliament and legislatures in our progress toward constitutional renewal, but would also help ensure that Parliament will play its full and rightful role in the building of the Canada of the future.

speechtext:
Judging by the Prime Minister's statement and the public comments of other participants, it appears that the first ministers' meeting yesterday made a reasonable start on the process of constitutional change and there is no question that all members of the House applaud that progress.
June 10, 1980

As I understand it, the Prime Minister sought agreement on a statement of principles as well as on process, and the goal of agreement on a statement of principles was not reached. It may not even have been pressed by the Prime Minister after he noted the reaction of other first ministers. Consequently-and I think it important that the House and the country understand this fact-the document relating to principles which the Prime Minister has tabled represents only a proposal by the federal government and not an agreement by the meeting.
The Prime Minister made reference to my speech of Friday. He learned long ago the value to him of reading my speeches and adopting my policy, and 1 recommend that speech to him as well.
I must say that I am a little surprised by the Prime Minister's assertion in his statement that "all of the first ministers committed themselves to a September deadline for major decisions". My understanding from the public comments of the premiers is that many of them see the September meeting as an opportunity to conclude whatever agreement has been reached by ministers and officials in the intervening months, but that they do not regard September as a deadline for decision on all items in the list. Indeed, Premier Blakeney is reported as saying: "We agreed unanimously there should be no deadline for reform"; and if that is so it was a wise decision by the first ministers, because agreement on complex and fundamental questions is work that is too important to be jeopardized by artificial deadlines.
Premier Blakeney went on to say: "We also agreed unanimously if we meet in September and accomplish nothing, it won't look very good"; and certainly the House would hope that discussions this summer will result in an agreement on several specific matters. The question of the nature of the agreement yesterday and the nature of the goals for September affects the expectations that will surround the September meeting, and I hope the Prime Minister will indicate later whether, in his view, the other first ministers are committed to agreement, in principle, in September, on any, on all or on most of the 12 items in the list.

1 also noted the following words of the Prime Minister:
-the federal government would have to give serious consideration to its options and recommend to Parliament a plan of action-
-if there is no agreement on the short list of items.
Mention was made of the use of a federal referendum to try to force acceptance of some changes the federal government wants, and we would like to know if that is what the Prime Minister really means or what other unilateral initiatives he is contemplating.
I should like to add that if the federal government expects a co-operative attitude from the provinces with regard to constitutional reform, it must be co-operative itself about other matters that are of importance to some provinces. The Prime Minister knows that 1 worry over the recent statements some of his ministers made and that I fear they will ruin the
Constitutional Renewal
atmosphere of good will that will be necessary for constitutional reform.

In closing, I want to express my satisfaction and that of my party that the first ministers have agreed on a busy agenda for the summer, and to express also the hope that the discussion will be pursued in a genuine atmosphere of co-operation and lead to significant agreement by September.

The participants showed their good will yesterday. The same attitude must continue to prevail this summer. And of course, Madam Speaker, some decisions will finally have to be taken at the September conference. I agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in that regard. Quebeckers and Canadians of other areas have been waiting long enough for a new Canadian constitution that would allow Quebeckers to prosper within Canada and would recognize as well the legitimate regional grievances. I repeat that it is imperative that decisions be taken in September.

It is worth noting in the context of the decision-making process that my party has previously made known its constitutional position on the importance of including fundamental rights and language rights in a new constitution; on the need to leave with the federal government certain financial powers that will enable it to provide at long last an industrial strategy for this country from coast to coast; and on the need to improve our representative system in Ottawa so that those who live in both the west and in the east in particular will feel that they have a higher degree of effective and numerical representation here in the nation's capital.
For a number of months, Madam Speaker, a special 35-member committee of my party has been at work preparing detailed recommendations on the constitution and other matters, including all of the specifics in the short list that the Prime Minister tabled today. I am pleased to say, Madam Speaker, that on these matters we have made decisions for a series of meetings that will take place over the summer as well, and we as a party will be ready for the September first ministers' conference with very specific suggestions for consideration at that time.

Having made these general observations about the substantial progress that now seems to be under way, I want to conclude with a minor but critical observation. No other democratic nation in the modern world has left to such a small number of people-in this case 11-the serious task of making the decisions which will reshape the nature of a democratic state. While unquestionably wishing those 11 individuals every success, on behalf of my colleagues 1 should like to say that I profoundly wish that the people who met yesterday had found a more effective manner of involving substantially more Canadians in this very important democratic process.

I asked if the premiers would consider enlarging their delegations as we would enlarge ours by the addition of leaders of opposition parties. Once again, I do not want to speak for all of them or answer for each, but I think it is fair to say that they were quite negative to that proposal, which I believe is the attitude of the present Leader of the Opposition who thinks that it should be the job of the 11 ministers, at least in the early stages, to pursue these meetings and to head the delegations.

Is there some way we can work in the views of the Association of Mayors and Municipalities which have been expressed to the provincial governments and to the federal government for the last 30 years which would make it possible for the civil servants who will be working on this problem during the summer to consider some imaginative proposals on how both the federal and provincial governments can delegate some of their powers for temporary periods to these large cities or large regional governments to provide some evidence to this big mass of the Canadian people that we are trying to meet the needs of these many people who, for their own good reasons, want to live in the cities and yet have a place in the power structure without interfering with the constitutional powers of the federal or provincial governments? subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 would like to preface my remarks on this motion by saying that as a person with a science background and as a businessman, I carry no personal antagonism to metric per se. I recognize the need for rules and order in the business sections and sectors of the country and in the international marketplace.
My concern is with the approach used by the government to impose metric on the people of Canada. There are four basic points 1 want to make. First, there has been a lack of honouring the main tenets of the white paper tabled in January, 1970, on metric conversion in Canada. My second point is that it is unwise in metric conversion to make moves that are not in concert with the United States. Third, metric laws should make use of the metric system voluntary, as is the case in the United States. And fourth, the will of the people to make change has always been of prime importance in the parliamentary system. Metric conversion in Canada is being imposed and does not have the will and understanding of the people.
This country in 1871 passed the Metric Weights and Measures Act, which was an act to render permissive the use of the metric system. In 1873 the act was enlarged to the Weights and Measures Act. In January, 1970, a white paper on metric conversion was tabled in the House of Commons. It received the initial support of all parties. In April, 1971, the Weights and Measures Act was updated. I would like to quote one part of it:
All units of measurement used in Canada shall be determined on the international system of units established by the Government Conference of Weights and Measures.
This act authorized both a systems international metric system and customary Canadian units of measurement for trade. This act also contained a clause prohibiting governor in council amendment of schedule II of that act. To quote from the metric overview board report of February, 1980:
In essence, this act, which was proclaimed three years later, made SI the standard measurements units for Canada. But Canadian units of measurement were also authorized for use in trade as well as the special land measures for Quebec.
In June, 1971, the Metric Commission was established to advise the minister. In March, 1974, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) sent a letter to the premiers of the provinces advising that the plan of the Metric Commission had been endorsed by the government and asked the premiers for their assurance that the guideline dales were generally acceptable.
In March, 1975, there was a debate in this House on the motion to approve the guideline dates of the Metric Commission. Then in November, 1976, the omnibus bill. Bill C-23, was tabled in the House of Commons. This bill dealt with details
Metric System
pertaining to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, the Western Grain Stabilization Act, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, the Two-Price Wheat Act, hectare measurement in lieu of acres, Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, etc.
The metric overview board report points out that one of the provisions in the omnibus act was the repeal of the Weights and Measures Act which, in effect, allowed for metric only. This slipped through the eyes of Parliament. In effect, it meant the abolition of the Canadian Weights and Measures Act and removed from that act the early limitation of power of the governor in council to abolish Canadian units of measure in trade.
It is now obvious that members of Parliament were concerned and caught up in the details of the omnibus bill and missed the important and major play buried in the legislation at that time. All through the white paper of 1970 were warnings and cautions. I speak of the metric conversion white paper which I am holding in my hand. There were warnings and cautions that those planning metric conversion would have to be aware of the importance of the public understanding the reasons for metric conversion in Canada. I would refer hon. members to paragraphs 3.1(111), 3.2, 3.3, 5.2 and 4.8.3, which carried these warnings throughout this report.
In 1977 the other place issued warnings in its hearings, which were again ignored, concerning metric conversion in Canada. It is my opinion that the government, the Metric Commission and its officials failed to accept the wisdom of the white paper's concerns and warnings. They even failed to accept the warnings and admonitions of the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) who spoke in the debate in March, 1975. I trust that one of my colleagues speaking later to this motion will be good enough to cover some of the points made by the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in that debate. They got themselves entrenched in planning, in engineering, in kiosks, in details and with legislative intrigue and, in this process, forgot about the Canadian people, the need to have the people understand the "why" of metric conversion in Canada and the importance of people accepting the change.
As I stand to speak in this debate a decade later, there is no "why" for metric conversion in Canada. The case put forth in the white paper has not withstood the test of time. We have had the right to use metric in Canada since 1871. Am I the only person in this House who finds the patchwork, piece by piece, step by step use of this Parliament to impose the SI system of hard metric conversion on the people of Canada rather strange and frightening?
The failure of the Metric Commission to heed all aspects of the white paper became evident when a large number of Canadians expressed their deep antagonism and resentment about metric conversion to the candidates competing for office in the 1979 election.
As we came out of the 1979 election we had a situation where the imposition of metric conversion on the people by the

June 10, 1980
Metric System
Liberal government, through the heavy-handed actions of its commission and federal inspectors, was a direct affront to the majority of the people and to the parliamentary system.
The whole approach of the Metric Commission and the Liberal government has turned out to be one of planning the imposition of metric on the people through the use of indirect authority, indirect amendment to key legislation, interdepartmental intrigues, removal of legislative safeguards-all in the spirit of well organized stealth and contempt for the people and their Parliament.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
As we enter the constitutional debate on the centralization of powers, let us be aware of the hazards to our freedom by centralizing powers into commissions, tribunals and the bureaucracy, as against increasing the power of Parliament by improving its institutions and structures. The latter will allow for reactions from the people and will preserve freedoms through the continuous process of change while the former will surely lead us into a form of democratic dictatorship. It should anger us all when bureaucrats who are supposed to be apolitical professionals in their service to the Crown engage in political partisanship through official government communications.
I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, and the attention of my colleagues, to a memorandum regarding the main estimates, 1980-81, from the Metric Commission of Canada to the minister which reads, in part, as follows:
The completion of the final or implementation phase has been delayed by the decision of the former cabinet to postpone the conversion of scales in the retail food sector.
The memorandum continues in another paragraph as follows:
Previous favourable public response to the Metric Commission's information and awareness activities recently has been damaged by the actions of the previous government, and considerable remedial work is required. Gallup poll surveys in 1973 and 1977 and a July 15, 1978, Weekend Magazine poll reflected the growing favourable trend towards SI. Latent negative reactions to the changeover, brought out and exacerbated by the previous government's actions and statements, show up in a November 1979 Gallup poll-
That is misleading in the extreme, Mr. Speaker, because the downward trend in popularity of metric had taken place over a period of four years, if you look at unbiased polls and surveys.
Another comment in this memorandum to which I take exception is the misleading information it gives the minister when it states as follows:
-now published will have been implemented as this country joins the rest of the world in converting to the full use of the international system of units (SI).
Singapore and Australia use SI units and there might be one other country. We are rushing to join the whole world? I suggest there is a bias in the Metric Commission that is extremely dangerous to the parliamentary process.
Let me return to the matter of trade, Mr. Speaker. If we consult the white paper on metric conversion in Canada, one of the main reasons it gives to justify metric conversion is trade.
It tells us that we have to join 110 countries that are using metric. Paragraph 4.2.1. of the white paper reads as follows:
The marked trend to the metric system outside North America, and the increasing importance to Canada of export markets, especially for manufactured goods, make it urgently necessary to consider the matter of conversion. The question is a complex one because the United States, which is Canada's main export market, has not made a decision to convert.
Paragraph 4.6.1. reads as follows:
Important benefits of conversion are to be found in ability to maintain and expand Canadian trade with nations in the metric sphere. Because of the vital importance of foreign trade to Canada, especially the need for growth in exports of manufactured goods, there must be serious concern about damage to Canada's competitiveness in world markets as a result of the pace of changeover to the metric system in the world at large.
I could go on, as there are several other sections which refer to trade. One decade later we find that only 4.8 per cent of our trade is with metric countries-Australia and Singapore-who have converted to the SI system. But that is not where our export trade is. We buy from them. The major western trading countries, the United Kingdom, the United States of America and Canada, still trade in standard measure. It should be pointed out that 75 per cent of Canada's trade is with the United States.
For Canada to rush into hard SI metric ahead of our major export markets is, in my opinion, just economic suicide. Certain sectors have changed voluntarily to metric and have been encouraged to do so. General Motors has sought international standards and it is in their interest to do so. Nobody argues with that. There is no problem in the pre-packaged area of consumer merchandise, except where hard metric, on top of bilingual labelling, becomes a non-trade tariff barrier to protect monopoly interests. There are interests in Canada that have been counting on this.
The white paper also says:
It would be wise to allow the timing and process of conversion to be closely related to the development of United States practice.
Paragraph 4.5.2. of the white paper states:
Where export to widely dispersed foreign markets is important, as in certain forest industries, the urge is strong to seek maximum international standardization.
They must have been thinking of the pulp and paper sector of that great industry because the approach imposed has escalated costs in the balance of the industry.
Sector conversion was to be voluntary. The white paper emphasized that and the Metric Commission reports and all their propaganda emphasize that it is voluntary. Yet through the calculated impression given by the Prime Minister's letter to the premiers in 1974, the province of British Columbia changed all forestry measures to metric without consulting the forest industries. We now have even the province of British Columbia backing off metric.
I should like to quote from a report by the government of British Columbia on March 11 to a meeting of the intergovernmental metric conversion committee, which says on page 3:
I do not wish to belabour the point, but our Interministerial Metric Conversion Committee has unanimously expressed grave concern to the Metric Commission that the failure to properly inform the public will result in unnecessary
June 10, 1980

future delays, public resentment and hostility. This matter was also the subject of discussion in the legislature of the province of British Columbia.
On page 4 it states:
There is a vast difference between the public being made vaguely aware that something is happening, and being positively informed of what is taking place, the reason for it and how it will affect them.
That is the dilemma in Canada. It goes on to say:
I suggest it is a rare individual in Canada who is not aware that we are converting to metric. However, the public have not been informed what that system is and the reason for the change.
The failure to inform the public, interpreted by many as intentional bureaucratic withholding of information, has caused serious apprehension and resentment which eventually led to the establishment of the overview committee. Rumblings of discontent by retailers, consumers and the general public have already surfaced. They could well develop into groundswell or even tidal waves of resistance if preventive measures are not taken.
That is what we were involved in when we ordered the overview board to make a report on the condition and the efficiency of metric conversion in Canada.
Except for the pulp and paper sector of the forest industry where definition of weights and measures is of little importance, we find that there is some $2.5 billion of forest products sold to world markets all in standard measure. Germany wants plywood in standard measure, such as 4 x 8 sheets. The United States uses standard measure. Sixty-five per cent of our lumber market in British Columbia is with the United States. The new Russian plywood mill has 4x8 sheets. Yet in the face of such trade facts we have the government trying to force the forest industry to go hard SI metric.
The type of pressure being applied is centralized federal power at its best-perhaps I should say at its worst, I stand corrected. No wonder the frontier provinces are concerned. In 1978 Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation refused to consider mortgage assistance unless plans were drawn in metric measure. Some time this year we will be looking at a new national building code entirely in metric, regardless of the fact that there is almost no hard metric dimension lumber or plywood in the country. Forty-two per cent of the construction dollar is a government dollar. Plans and bids have to be metric to win these bids. What does the winning bidder do? He makes his bid and submits his drawings in hard metric. He then converts his drawings to Canadian standard measure so that whatever is being built can be built within acceptable cost limits. The same happens with Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages for houses. The metric overview board recommended that the forest industry should remain in standard measure in Canada until, or if, an agreement with the United States is made. To change to another form of measure is insane. I suggest that that sector, as others with similar problems, be allowed to remain in soft metric measure.
I understand that the HUDAC group are lobbying members today and have recommended that the process of metric conversion be continued and that a clear and concise statement from the federal government be made setting forth the government's full support of the metric conversion program without introducing legislation. I completely disagree with their stance
Metric System
because it ignores the will and the expression of consumers in Canada and the majority of the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: Talk to the builders and the insurance companies about it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
A unilateral move by Canada will create two inventories, two sets of plans and unnecessary costs that can only weaken the economic strength of the country. All of this turmoil in the forest industry has occurred in spite of the warnings carried in the white paper. The white paper made it very clear that we must consider the progress of conversion in the United States, and that we should be in concert with that progress.
Paragraph 4.5.4 says that we should not attempt conversion independently of the United States. Paragraph 4.6.5 says that timing and process is to be closely related to the development of United States practice. Other warnings were carried in paragraphs 4.6.7, 4.6.8 and 4.8.2.
In 1975 the United States passed their metric act. At least the U.S. system works, and when the United States does something it is put up to their elected representatives for a debate. Heavy emphasis on that act was on voluntary compliance. The United States is still a democracy reflecting and respecting the people's concern. The spirit of the U.S. metric act is that its federal government is ready and willing to assist voluntary moves.
There is a great difference between the Canadian voluntary program and the voluntary program of the United States. The Canadian government has played with the word and with the legislation. Under the Canadian voluntary program we have been orchestrated. The development of sector plans has been by the government. People have been talked into it. We have had paid sector officials who repeated and repeated the fact that metric was now law.
Grass roots consumer organizations, such as the Consumers' Association of Canada, in my opinion, have been co-opted. Could it be that the $450,000 a year which it gets from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has had an effect? That organization was a grass roots organization that really created the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs out of grass roots consumer concerns. Yet where has its voice been when the dairy industry of Ontario and of other provinces converted to metric, and milk and dairy products have cost the consumer 12 per cent more as a result of the conversion?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: Nary a word from them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
On the other hand, in the United States there is a metric board and a metric act. The metric commission in the United States is supported by the private sector. It has no powers other than to assist where the change is desired. The voluntary initiatives have been in areas where it does not affect the consumer. In my opinion, it is foolish to force metric

June 10, 1980
Metric System
ahead of its time. The evolutionary process will take care of that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: In Canada, pressure has been exerted. Small business has had to follow big business. There has been no consensus in major sectors that have been involved in the Canadian brand of voluntary conversion. We found that out in the meat packing industry after we were in office for a short time, and we found it also in the retail sector of the food industry. There was no consensus in those voluntary sectors.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: And no consultation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
There was leverage, use of regulation, use of inspectors and back room deals. The government has played games with governor in council powers, with legislation, with the provinces and with Parliament. The government has seen fit to impose system international metric on the people without a sustainable reason for it.
Canadian conversion is nine to 15, maybe even 20 years ahead of the United States. The Liberal government, with its fetish for secrecy, has not even published the metric overview board's report which is a valuable overview on the whole area of public concern.
Freedom of information is a serious issue as we watch the Liberals try to centralize more and more power into the bureaucracies and its tribunals and commissions. I have always thought that limited government was a cornerstone of Liberal-Conservative political principle. That is not the case here.
As an aside, the hard-working members of the metric overview board have not yet been paid for the valuable work they have performed. That is a twist that is below the normal sense of decency and fair play expected of professional, apolitical civil servants.
I urge the government to table or publish the metric overview board report. It is a valuable document for the metric debate. All that is published is this Metric Monitor which is a biased, one-sided view of the debate. It is straight propaganda done with the people's money. In the metric overview board report you have the other side of the coin. This matter can be opened up and perhaps understood in a more equitable, fair-share way.
The democratic way would be to have a metric act fully debated in the House of Commons so that all the pieces are together in one place in one play and all concerned could make input to the process. The debate we are in today is the manipulation, by stealth, of legislation and regulation to make the standard measurement system illegal in Canada.
What has happened in Canada and Great Britain is that too much power has been gained by the bureaucracy and the academic elite. Our challenge is to strengthen the parliamentary institutions so that the skills and knowledge of the academic elite cun be used and enhanced, but with the ultimate power and control remaining with the collective expression of the people.
If we allow the government and its bureaucracy to deny the expression and will of the people due process, then we in this House have pulled the curtain down on the parliamentary process and we in Canada are dangerously close to another form of government. The insensitivity and arrogance of those responsible for metric conversion in Canada attacks the heart of our system.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on my way to the House this afternoon, realizing that this opposition day dealt with the metric system, I looked down at my feet while walking through the tunnel and thought how history had been cheated. Had that king some x number of hundreds of years ago who sat on the throne of Great Britain huge feet like mine, three of them would have made exactly one metre and we would not have this argument this afternoon. However, such was not the case and today we have a very real concern in this country over the change from one system to another.
A number of questions and concerns have been put to me. When 1 first came here, one of the first things I did was list what I heard during the campaign. I was never sure how many were legitimate questions, how many were myths and how many were straight propaganda. I had a little study carried out on these questions. The questions I asked were: How did we get the metric system introduced in Canada? Was it done democratically?
In the minds of the population there seem to be a lot of metric systems utilized around the world. That is the impression you get when you read the pro and con letters to the editor in the small weeklies in my area. Are there in fact several types of metric? If so, which kind are we going to adopt for ourselves?
Of what use is the system? We are told that our trading partners mostly use the imperial system. Is that true? Who benefits from changing to metric? Who pays? Are these legitimate concerns or are they myths in the minds of the population?
I had a study carried out; I am not sure how objective it is. The questions were answered by the staff of the Parliamentary Library who tested out the legal basis and so on. I will review some of the answers that were found.
The legal basis for our system is the Weights and Measures Act passed in April, 1971. It became law on August 1 of that year. It allows the use of the metric system in commerce and trade in Canada. In review, a white paper on metric conversion was tabled by the government in January of 1970. The leaders of all parties in the House gave their support to the policy as outlined in the white paper.
Subsequently in June, 1971, the government established the Metric Commission by order in council and in 1974 approved
June 10, 1980

the national program of guideline dates for metric conversion, consisting of four distinct phases. Phase one, investigation of the system, was to be completed by 1974. Phase two, the planning stage, was to be completed by 1975. Phase three, which dealt with scheduling, was to have been completed in 1976. Phase four, implementation, was to begin in 1975.
In March, 1975, the Hon. Alastair Gillespie, then minister of industry, trade and commerce, introduced a resolution to the House of Commons to approve the government's program of guideline dates for metric conversion. The resolution was referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs which examined and endorsed the program, and recommended that further legislation to facilitate metric conversion be enacted; as well, the ministers responsible for metric conversion in each of the provinces unanimously endorsed it in 1976. I was a little surprised to find these facts recorded in light of some of the comments made since.
The government announced its intention to introduce a series of four omnibus bills to modify the approximately 90 existing laws governing weights and measures and to allow for conversion to metric. The first of these bills, the statute law, the Metric Conversion Amendment Act, was introduced in the House of Commons on November 22, 1976. The act included amendments to several existing pieces of legislation including the Weights and Measures Act, the act of 1971. That act had previously stipulated that the governor in council could not amend schedule II to the act so as to prevent the use of customary Canadian units of measurement in trade. The amendments, however, removed that prohibition. Moreover, the amendments gave the governor in council power to make regulations setting a date beyond which any units of measurement set out in schedule II could not be used in trade. In effect, this allowed the phasing out of the use of Canadian units, as established in schedule II of the act, in favour of the metric units in schedule I for use in trade. That, briefly, is how we got into the situation we are now in.
Pursuant to the act, orders in council were passed relating to the use of metric units in the retailing of gasoline and diesel fuel, individually measured food and scale conversion, and home furnishings. Subsequently, an order in council removed the requirement that metric units of measurement be used in the retailing of individually measured food and that retail scales for such foods use metric units. Again, that occurred on January 18, 1980.
The system that we are moving toward is the system of international units, symbolized by SI, the system often referred to simply as the metric system. There seems to be a great deal of confusion about SI and whether there are any other metric systems. Perhaps the main source of confusion may be in the fact that different countries at different points in time have chosen to define their measurements in relation to different base units. Thus we have systems such as the so-called CGS system-which stands for centimetre, gram and second-and in other countries we have the so-called MKS
Metric System
system, which stands for metre, kilogram and second. Both systems have existed for a long time. These systems are different only in that base units and their legal definitions vary. One system may be based on the gram, another system based on the kilogram. Basically the metre in either country will be the same length, the gram will be the same weight. So they differ only in legal definition; the size of the units are integral, the same from country to country.
It has been necessary to review SI from time to time to add, replace or redefine certain measurements in order to keep up with technological and scientific requirements. This does not usually have any effect on trade or commerce. It is simply a way of more clearly defining the length of the metre for scientific purposes. For instance, to begin with the metre was considered-improperly, as it turned out-to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator on the meridian that goes through Paris, France. Advanced measuring techniques later showed that this was not quite correct. The current definition of a metre-and I think this is the latest definition-is that it is 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of orange-red light radiated by the isotope krypton-86 as measured in a vacuum. Even that very lengthy definition may have to be redesigned as more precise terms are available, now that we have laser technology. In any event, while the metre has had several different definitions it has remained the same size throughout the world regardless of the legal definition.
How international is the system? Forty-five countries, including Canada, have signed the Treaty of the Metre of 1875 which requires that they express their units of measurement in terms of SI units and support financially the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sevres, France. These member countries also form the General Conference on Weights and Measures which oversees the advancement of SI. In addition many countries have converted or are in the process of converting to the use of SI measurements. Indeed, of the 154 countries recognized by the United Nations, 152 use some or all of the SI system in measurement, with only North and South Yemen remaining totally outside the use of SI measurement. The SI units adopted by Canada will be the same as those used in all other countries which have accepted these SI definitions as set out by the General Conference.
Who benefits from metric conversion? Well, as a general statement of principle I think one could say that the large international manufacturers benefit first from international conversion. To present proof I simply turn to the case of General Motors, one of the largest international corporations. In 1960 General Motors estimated the cost of conversion at about $1 billion. In 1973 this estimate was revised to approximately 11 per cent of that amount and the decision was made to proceed with metrication within General Motors. That was without legal coercion; it was a decision made at their head office in the United States. In 1979 they found that the actual cost of going metric in all divisions appeared to be less than 1 per cent of their original 1960 estimate. Instead of $1 billion it was to cost 1 per cent of that, about $10 million.

June 10, 1980
Metric System
In the six years during which General Motors has been converted to metric they have found that the cost avoidance, or savings, have overshadowed the cost of conversion by a factor of ten or 15 to one, so that instead of costing them money it was making them money. General Motors' metric plan goes like this: first, new development would be metric from the start. This would include items in the current development stage. This was the plan in 1973. Second, service parts and in-production parts would be left alone. Third, supplier coordination would be implemented; that is to say, suppliers would be worked into the metric system as well. Fourth, their capital equipment would be purchased with dual measuring capability where applicable. The result is that today 27 passenger car series in the General Motors line of domestically made automobiles are predominantly metric. Only seven remaining series have not been fully redesigned since the initiation of the metric policy in 1973, and it is anticipated that these, too, will be metric by the early 1980s.
It should be noted that General Motors' primary purpose in adopting this metric policy was to enable it to design, manufacture and market similar or identical products or components all over the world. This is a point which has not been lost on my local constituents. They realize that companies like General Motors get advantages from going metric. They realize that General Motors would have probably gone metric whether Canada did or did not. Their objection is on the grounds that a great many aspects of our commerce and our economy in this country and certainly in a lot of the smaller towns and villages offer really no incentive to switch to metric. The consumers are used to the old system, they have measuring equipment geared to handle the old system and to them the new system appears only to be a cost with no benefits. We have a whole generation of people who could be considered to be a non-metric generation.
Our school system and our educational institutions are busily turning out a new generation that were trained to conceptualize things in metric terms. My children, for instance, do not really conceive of inches, or even pounds. They speak in centimetres and metres. When 1 do little chores with them, help them build a playhouse or something, the length of the piece of wood 1 hand them, or ask them to saw, has to be converted so that I may tell them it is so many centimetres or so many metres long. This forces people in my generation to become familiar with the metric system.
My automobile has dual systems on the speedometer. I have used this to great effect in learning how many kilometres there are in so many miles. I now have more or less a grasp of how far 60 kilometres is, or how far 100 kilometres is. It is starting to mean something to me. But I know there are a great many more people in my communities who were not brought up to worry about the metric system.
To put it dramatically, one fellow presenting a petition to me said that just with this move to metric the government has made his whole education and his whole lifetime of experience
obsolete. His whole method of conceptualizing things has been made totally out of date, and he has been left almost in an alien society. I am not talking about western alienation, Quebec separatism or anything like that, but about a whole generation or generation and a half of our citizens who are being alienated through our attempt to move our retail trade at the local level too quickly toward metric. I think we should take a second look at that and slow it down a little bit, because we are asking a great deal of these people when we ask them to throw 50 or 60 years of their experience in the trash bin, so to speak.
We have asked farmers to make a sort of double switch by going from bushels to the tonne, because by taking that step we have gone through two forms of conceptualization. We must remember that the bushel was essentially and is essentially, if it still exists anywhere, a measure of volume. A bushel of wheat weighs 60 pounds. A bushel of oats weighs 34 pounds. When we measure things in tonnes, the old measurements do not work any more.
We have to apply varying numbers to the kinds of grain that we put into granaries which once held 1,000 bushels. We have gone from a volume system to a weight system, and then we have not used the kind of weight system with which we were familiar. We were familiar with pounds or tons, but we have moved to kilograms and tonnes. It has been a double shift, and it has been very hard for many farm people to catch up.
To be honest, it has created some problems for the grain trade. How can we measure the capacity of an elevator system which was laid out in bushels and cubic measurements when now we have to use tonnes? We knew the bushel capacity available in an elevator which might have held 100,000 bushels. Now that capacity varies depending on the kind of grain that goes into it. It will hold 6,000 tonnes of wheat but only 3,400 tonnes of oats. There are seven or eight kinds of grains that you could put in between with weights that vary. There are very sophisticated statistical methods for bodies like the Canadian Wheat Board or the Canadian Grains Commission by which they can plug in their computers and get a more or less accurate assessment of how much space there will be at any of the delivery points, given the kinds of delivery patterns that have existed.
However, it is still not the same as knowing how much volume there is out there. If the delivery patterns of farmers change from oats to wheat, for instance, the capacity is reduced almost by one-half without the computer or the managers of the Canadian Wheat Board even knowing about it. So it has created new ways of having to deal with old problems.
I think we ended up holding on to the acre as the basic unit of measurement in western Canada, simply because our land was already surveyed in discrete amounts. There is one mile between lines. This creates a certain number of acres, 640 to the square mile. True, we can make estimations. We can say 800 metres is approximately half a mile and 800 metres squared gives us about 64 hectares, which is only one hectare short of a full quarter section. It is close enough for figuring,
June 10, 1980

but it is still stupid to go into the land titles offices and change all the titles just to fit into the metric system of measurement. Since my time is almost expired, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like just to reiterate that we in rural Canada can see that large scale corporations do not have any disincentive to switch to metric. We can see the large scale food industries switching to metric because to them there is no real cost. Their equipment handles a large enough volume of weighing and measuring that it wears out occasionally, and they can use that five-year or six-year changeover to put in metric scales at really no cost to them. But we have little businesses, even some fair-sized ones like the Wynyard Co-op, which estimates it is going to cost $25,000 just to switch over to weighing and metering under a metric system if it becomes something that it must do.
We understand that some of this will happen whether the law changes or not. We realize that General Motors will be producing metric cars, but we cannot see why small retailers have to switch to the system cold turkey, if you like, leaving the old imperial measurement system completely in the background. We think those scales have been working. We think their traditional customers have been used to using those weights and measurements, and we think this should at least be allowed to go on in concert with the new changes.
1 make one last plea. Let us reconsider that generation of people who feel completely alienated by the change. They have their rights, they are part of this country, they have made their contribution and 1 think they should be considered in the next few years. Let us slow down the change and be more humanistic.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State, Small Businesses):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), I would like to make a few comments on existing acts pertaining to the metric system, and the way Canada has been approaching metrication since the white paper was brought forward in 1970.
But before coming to specific remarks, I would like to remind the hon. member for Capilano that I took a good note of the memorandum he referred to, and indicate to him my undertaking to study it. Because on the principle he stated, that it was at least strange that government advisers took it upon themselves to criticize openly a decision taken by a government elected by the people, I would like to tell him I took good note of his remarks and I will try to get more details on the subject.
However, and this also concerns the speech made by the hon. member for Capilano, 1 would like to stress how much I was shocked when he referred to payments due the two members of the overview board. At least ten days ago, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member sat next to me here in this House, as is normally done between civilized people, to ask me to try to expedite within my department the last two payments due the two members of the metric overview board. This happened ten days ago. Unfortunately, I had to stay away from the
Metric System
House for a week, and when I returned yesterday, I already had from officials in the department I am representing an answer indicating the procedure to expedite these last two payments. And not later than noontime today, an official of my staff phoned the office of the hon. member for Capilano to inform him 1 was now in a position to expedite the last payments, as I intended to do within the next few days. I think mentioning those details in his speech while implying the government wanted by that to show its disagreement with the report of the metric overview board was not at all fair play. With respect to the release of the report of the metric overview board, the hon. member for Capilano should understand-and 1 also mentioned to him at the time 1 personally looked at that report for the first time on April 18, 1978, and as this is a 375-page report-that there must be delays due not only to the consideration of the report but also due to the translation of such a big document.
Mr. Speaker, I found it indeed very interesting to hear the comments of the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) who explained, without bombast, contrary to what his predecessor did, basing himself on examples drawn from everyday life experience in his area, that metrication or the conversion from the imperial system to the international system was obviously causing certain problems with a certain category of Canadians whom he called very rightly "the non-metric generation." I agree with the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre that above all must be consideration for those people; the system I think is necessary, as indeed the leaders of the three parties recognized in this House in 1970 when the white paper was tabled. Even if the system is necessary in the short, medium and long terms, it is quite obvious that we must not above all metricate to metricate but rather take into consideration in the first place the interests of the users, the consumers and the industries affected by the changes that result from metrication.
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us implies that the Canadian economy needs other legislation on the metric system. I want, for my part, to remind the House that of the 88 sectors that released sector plans, only three, namely the sale of gasoline by the litre, furniture and balances in the retail food business, are regulated under the 1971 Weights and Measures Act which was later amended, as was mentioned, by the 1976-77 act.
Only in those three cases, Mr. Speaker, did the industries concerned ask, with the support of the Consumers' Association of Canada, for pertinent regulations throught the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. 1 would like, at this point, Mr. Speaker, to make a brief remark on the Consumers' Association of Canada because 1 was most surprised to hear the hon. member for Capilano mention or suggest that this association, which has so vigorously and competently defended the interests of Canadian consumers, may have been prevented from expressing honestly its views because of possible grants it

June 10, 1980
Metric System
may have received. 1 am taken aback by this judgment on the Consumers Association of Canada. As 1 already mentioned, some sectors are also under provincial jurisdiction and some fertilizers and pesticides are subject to the Fertilizers Act and the Pest Control Products Act of the federal government. Most of the other approximately 80 sectors convert without legislation in accordance with the guidelines, standards and target dates prepared by over 2,000 voluntary workers from all sectors of the Canadian economy, including unions, consumers and teachers.
A brief comment on some economic sectors might help to illustrate, Mr. Speaker, how the Canadian economy as a whole is adapting to metric conversion without requiring any legislation. Let us take for instance the manufacturers of motor vehicles and parts, which include the companies which manufacture or assemble motor vehicles, such as automobiles, commercial vehicles, buses and trucks. This sector also includes the manufacturers of motor vehicle parts and accessories such as motors, brakes, clutches, axles, gears, and so on.
Metric conversion for private vehicle manufacturers was implemented at the same time in Canada and the United States. The metric contents of 1980 models manufactured by the different companies vary from 90 per cent for General Motors, to 48 per cent for Ford and 34 per cent for Chyrsler. General Motors has publicly stated that it intends to complete conversion of its operations by 1982.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Alt-house) may be right in saying that, in any case, these companies would probably have converted to the metric system with or without a metric conversion program, but it is important to note that this major sector of the economy undertook this process on a voluntary basis such as recommended in the white paper of 1970. Private vehicles and parts manufacturers are expected to complete their conversion program in December, 1982, according to the target date and to the metric conversion plan published in 1976. Truck manufacturers should have completed their metric conversion program by 1990.
Another sector which we could study for a little while would be forestry. Most research establishments in the forest industry are now operating completely in metric units. All forest inventories are now being carried out in metric measurements. As of January 1, 1979, metric scaling was used in British Columbia and Alberta and is expected to come into force in Ontario as of April 1, 1981. The national standard for scaling roundwood is now being used to some degree by most provinces. Training programs for woods personnel are under way across the country. The forestry sector has now completed 98 per cent of the activities in its plan and is expected to be essentially metric by mid-1980.
Another sector which would be of interest to members is the petroleum and natural gas industries and services. Metric
conversion in the oil and gas industries is another example of a conversion which has proceeded relatively smoothly. This has been brought about by the leadership exhibited by the Canadian Petroleum Association. The association, realizing the necessity to formulate a well-thought-out plan for the industry, established a committee in 1972 with the responsibility of bringing about an orderly transition to the metric system on a least cost basis. This sector committee is truly representative of the industry, with representatives from all phases of the petroleum production field. Operations have been essentially in metric since January, 1979.
Before leaving these remarks on sectors, 1 would like to touch briefly on the plastics industry. At present, a substantial number of plastics manufacturers are marketing their products in metric units. Further progress towards metric conversion is expected as more companies are identifying their products in metric terms in response to market demands. Blow moulders of plastic containers experience no difficulties in meeting market demands for plastic metric containers. Metric production is also on the way in the reinforced plastic composites, injection moulding, machinery and mould-maker areas of the industry, in response to market demands. The ultimate objective is international standardization. Conversion is to be compatible with related domestic and worldwide industries and achieved at minimal cost. The plastics industry as a whole is expected to operate predominantly in metric by July, 1983.
The motion before us also suggests that it is the government which has somehow managed to impose the metric system on the people of Canada. The motion suggests that this House of Commons has somehow avoided the metric system, while the government has somehow failed to consult the representatives of the people.

The policy conclusion stated in the white paper was that metric conversion was inevitable and in the national interest.
