speechtext:
If hon. members opposite are not happy with those comments, I should like to indicate that those are the comments made by the hon. member for Capilano when he said what happened in the House concerning the metric system. If they are not happy, they do not have to listen; they can work on something else.
On April 7, 1971, the Weights and Measures Act was amended and recognized the "systeme international" as the
June 10, 1980

legal metric system for use in Canada. The "systeme international" is the latest evolution of the metric system and has been in use for close to 100 years. On June 10, 1971, the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act made a metric contents declaration mandatory for all pre-packaged goods. A program of guideline dates for metric conversion was approved by the government and debated by the House of Commons of March 17, 1975. The Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs studied this matter at length and reported back to the House of Commons on December 17, 1976, with a recommendation that the House consider the advisability of adopting this program and also introduce additional legislation to facilitate metric conversion.
Subsequently Bill C-23, which became the Statute Law (Metric Conversion) Amendment Act of 1976, was debated in the House of Commons and the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs over a period of almost ten months. Exchanges took place on the floor of the House of Commons and in the Senate 16 times. It was passed by the House of Commons on July 15. 1977, and received royal assent on August 5, 1977. In view of these debates and discussions over the years, one can only conclude that the motion as presented is not based on the facts.
Now I should like to deal with the Canadian approach to metric conversion. To perform its task. Metric Commission Canada established 12 steering committees, each responsible for co-ordinating a group of economic sectors that have related interests. For example, steering committee No. 5 groups the following sectors: construction, non-metallic mineral products, structural and architectural metals, engineers, real estate, land surveyors and town planners. Canadians working in all types of organizations sit on the various steering committees representing the Canadian people and co-ordinating the conversion activities of all sectors of Canadian society. The commission established 100 sector committees which report to the steering committees. Each is responsible for a particular industry, group of industries or interests. These sector committees are preparing the basic plans for converting the sector for which they are responsible. They are doing this in collaboration with the individual firms and individual associations.
The ongoing task of the steering committees and their sector committees is to monitor the progress of conversion and suggest any necessary modifications to the plans in order to meet changing conditions. These sector plans are guides for the individual firms and organizations concerned. While there is no obligation on any firm to conform to them, they represent the best judgment of the industry on how to go about the process of conversion. Since individual firms and public service organizations are the entities that are implementing metric conversion, it is clear they have a major role to play in the national conversion process.

speechtext:
The basis of the Canadian approach to metric conversion is that it is a voluntary process, each firm and organization being guided by its appreciation of its own short and long-term interests. As I indicated in my opening remarks, some regulations had to be passed by the House concerning three sectors, gasoline sale per litre, scaling in the retail trade and also some furniture articles. As I said, the basis of the Canadian approach is that of a voluntary process. A corollary of this approach is that each unit of the economy is expected to identify the opportunities for change and to bear its own costs, just as it will reap the benefits arising from the change.
There are obvious advantages to both Canada and the United States in programs for metric conversion that are reasonably co-ordinated. The United States Congress approved legislation providing for voluntary metric conversion. At the same time, industry in the United States is moving on a broad front to implement conversion programs. In the meantime, Canadian and American sector committees are stimulating, supporting and assisting all efforts to press forward with preparations for metric conversion. In the investigation phase in each industry or occupation, research is necessary to define the most appropriate metric units to be used, the metric standards to be employed, and the range of sizes or quantities to be used in metric production. In the planning phase the sequence of events and the time needed for this conversion process in each sector is determined and these tentative estimates are co-ordinated with the estimates of the requirements of suppliers and customers. In the scheduling phase a time table is developed for each industry and field of endeavour so that it can be co-ordinated with all other sectors within the over-all target date. The implementation phase is the final stage where each sector and individual organization implements the plans laid according to the schedule defined in the previous phase.
As was also mentioned, the government has consulted all the provinces as to how they wish to implement conversion in their areas of jurisdiction.
These include notably education, highway design and regulation and land title registration, besides many other important areas. Interdepartmental committees are established to plan and co-ordinate conversion work carried out in the different departments.
The metric system is legal for use in Canada and has been for a long time. Our Weights and Measures Act has been amended by Parliament through the Statute Law (Metric Conversion) Amendment Act of 1976 to allow the phasing in of the metric system in any sector of the economy at a time considered appropriate by a consensus of all concerned. In addition, most sectors of the economy are converting voluntarily after careful investigation, planning and scheduling of implementation. Therefore, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is

no need for any over-all legislation concerning the use of the metric system in Canada.

He was followed by the Hon. Tony Abbott. Those two former ministers did not listen to the thousands of Canadians who voiced an objection to metric in the retail food sector, and they are no longer with us today. Perhaps I am too benevolent in paying attention to the point which hon. members opposite fail to realize, that they do not pay attention to the consensus of the people of Canada or listen to their constituents when they voice their objections, not by tens, twenties or hundreds, but by thousands.
I have in my hand a computer print-out. It represents the number of people who have objected to the metric system. They are voters and constituents from across Canada. These files which I have on my desk are files of letters from constituents in Sherbrooke, Quebec, one of the test centres for metric in Canada. This file is a one-week file which is to be added to the thousands of letters from constituents and petitions from the riding of Peterborough, where there was a voluntary test centre.
I can tell hon. members how voluntary this system is and what the millions of people in Canada can expect on January 1, 1981. They can expect in 21 cities across this country a voluntary process, a process by which the metric commission dictates arbitrarily. Without consideration for the citizens of Canada, the merchants in 21 to 25 cities will buy metric scales, imported from the United States. The merchants, including the major food chain stores across Canada- Loblaws, Dominion Stores, Sunnybrook, IGA-will be told they must put in metric scales. They will then voluntarily
meter out the merchandise to the consumers who totally misunderstand the reasons for this implementation.
If hon. members opposite and the minister of small business, who I notice is not present in the House, fail to hear these comments and refuse to listen to the people of Canada about the implementation of metric by this so-called voluntary process, then I predict the minister will follow the line of Len Marchand and Tony Abbott who, as former ministers of small business, no longer have a seat in this House.
I enjoy my seat in this House. The former member who represented my riding was a member of the Liberal party. He was elected four times and was a cabinet minister. I refer to the Hon. Hugh Faulkner who represented Peterborough from 1965 to 1979. He did not listen to the constituents of Peterborough, nor did he respond to their concerns about the high cost of metric conversion at a time of unemployment and at a time when small businessmen were trying to make a living. He did not respond, listen, care, react; he did exactly the same thing as the present Minister of State for Small Businesses is doing. He completely disregarded the constituents in his riding, in Sherbrooke, in Kamloops and across Canada.
Hon. members opposite in that party which forms the government of the day, will enjoy reading the letters of the people who object to metric. At the bottom of this yardage of computer print-out there are approximately 12 names.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I respect your decision, but I would advise hon. members that 1 have no cardboard boxes. Perhaps you, sir, are referring to a member opposite or a member of the other opposition party.
During the question period on April 25 I asked the Minister of State for Small Businesses a question concerning the implementation of metric and whether there had ever been a full parliamentary discussion or an act formulated. At that time the minister said that there was no full legislation or implementation through an act of Parliament, in his memory, but he said he would look into that matter and advise me.
June 10, 1980

1 suppose it would be in order to read some of the concerns of the constituents which have brought them to my attention. Following a statement made in a speech during the Speech from the Throne debate in April, concerning the nightmare the metric implementation had brought to the people of Peterborough, a member opposite interrupted my remarks by saying there was not a single problem in Sherbrooke, not a single complaint. That remark is recorded in Hansard.
I took the liberty in finding out why metric, as it was implemented in Sherbrooke, Quebec, was such a roaring success when it was such a nightmare in Peterborough. I wrote a letter to the editor of the Sherbrooke paper-one of the two Anglophone papers in Quebec, I understand-saying 1 was very pleased to learn how successful the implementation of metric had been in Sherbrooke. I wrote that I would be very interested in learning from them why they related so favourably to this voluntary implementation program.
1 received more letters from Sherbrooke in ten days than 1 received in any ten-day period from my own constituents. They were totally unaware of the fact that it was implemented in Sherbrooke on a voluntary basis and totally unaware of the fact that it was implemented without a problem. I should like to read from one letter 1 received from a Sherbrooke constituent as follows:
You said you were surprised to be interrupted by the MP from Sherbrooke when you were commenting on metrication and that he said it was positive and there wasn't one complaint. Maybe he got no complaints. I don't know, but I doubt it . .. I have talked to many people in Sherbrooke and I haven't found one in favour of metrication.
Another letter reads as follows:
I was pleased to see your note in the Sherbrooke Record concerning the metric system. I am surprised the local MP stated there was no objection. 1 wish to state there is much dissatisfaction with the way the government has forced this on the public.
And yet another:
I cannot understand Mr. Pelletier stating that there was not a single complaint from the Sherbrooke area. The Dominion Store where I do most of my shopping took a survey, I think in February, and it was an overwhelming gesture against the metric system. I cannot see any benefit in the metric system, just a lot of confusion, and I can assure you the many housewives that I talk to are in agreement with me.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, it is not just the riding of Peterborough that is opposed to the implementation of forced metric. In January, Dominion Stores did a survey. The imperial measure was favoured by 88 per cent in Peterborough and by 68 per cent in Sherbrooke. The Dominion Stores study was a throrough one, a cross-section of detailed interviews of 3,000 people. In Peterborough, only 9.8 per cent of those interviewed favoured the metric system compared to 75 per cent for imperial. Those figures are for more than 2,000 interviews conducted in my riding by Dominion Stores. The figures speak for themselves.
Hon. members opposite may be able to totally ignore these figures and to say that the people of Canada will eventually learn to like it, but what about the food store owners?
Metric System
Allen C. Jackson, president of Dominion Stores Limited, in an interview I had with him followed by correspondence, said:
We are unable to find any significant benefit to the Canadian consumer at this time in using metric weights for fresh meats, fruits and vegetables. In fact, in the United States, which is our major trading partner, metrication is at least nine to ten years away.
Mr. Jackson's next comment, and 1 think it is a wise one, is that there is a clear need to delay metrication at least until the United States catches up to the Canadian rate of conversion.
I wonder if those on the other side of the House know how much money conversion will cost? Mr. Jackson says the cost to Dominion Stores alone for converting to metric sales is estimated to be $10 million.
Why should a company be forced to spend $10 million on metrication when it needed it for other purposes? Mr. Jackson says he would much prefer to spend the money on energy conservation. Why not spend this money on something like energy conservation? Could the Dominion Stores not spend $10 million in a better way, than in the United States to purchase weigh scales which Canada is unable to produce and supply? This has a negative effect on our balance of payments deficit.
It should be noted that it is not just the consumers of Canada who are up in arms over this issue. 1 had a letter from one storeowner in my riding who was particularly upset. He operates a store in Havelock, Ontario, which is on the eastern border of my riding. He indicated that his meat sales alone declined by 21 per cent from the implementation date of September 1, 1979, to November 24, 1979. He said the sales dropped because Havelock is only ten miles from Marmora and Campbellford which are still using imperial. Shoppers simply drove the few extra miles to shop in a system with which they were familiar. He estimated he had lost $37,000 at the time he wrote the letter, not including the $12,500 he had to spend for two metric scales imported from the United States.
Some hon. members may not believe there could be such heavy losses. As a businessman from the Peterborough area I can tell them there are, indeed, such losses. 1 should like to read an excerpt from another letter 1 received from a Peterborough constituent as follows:
I live in Peterborough, one of the three centres where the metric system is being shoved down our throats. I for one am defying the system and doing the larger portion of my shopping outside of the city and will continue to do so as long as I can find a merchant who will sell me 16 ounces to the pound and 12 inches to the foot.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, if the government will not respond or listen to the constituents of Canada, then perhaps the least we say on this side the better it will be for our party, because we will be returned with a majority, and will form a government that will listen to constituents, respond to their concerns and act accordingly.
This is not a voluntary system; this is a forced system. Two merchants have been locked up and forced out of business. Bands were wrapped around their weight scales so they could

June 10, 1980
Metric System
not sell one nickel's worth of their products until they purchased metric scales.
The implementation on January 1 in 21 cities will, I predict, cause a great upheaval across Canada. It should be put on record that Peterborough is not on the list of cities to face metrication on January 1. There is not one metric weight scale in any grocery store, chain or independent retail store in the riding of Peterborough today. That is what they think of metric implementation, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the debate this afternoon, one of the members suggested it might be useful to look at the question of metric in historic terms. I would like to do that very briefly.
The white paper on metric conversion, tabled in the House by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in January, 1970, put forward the view that metric conversion was inevitable and in the national interest. Among the advantages that were stated in the paper were ease and convenience in education and in general commerce, improved trading abilities and opportunities in world markets for Canadian industry.
In 1971, Metric Commission Canada was established to promote, plan and co-ordinate the change-over to the metric system in Canada and to advise the minister of industry, trade and commerce on legislative and any other action required to facilitate conversion to the metric system.
The commission consists of a number of part time commissioners, and the chairman, drawn from various segments of the economy and geographical regions of the country. In organizing their work, the commission divided the various elements of the economy into some 100 sectors and organized committees
to consider each of these. As a result, there are more than 2,000 persons, each of whom is knowledgeable in the particular subject involved, engaged in committee work. It is done on a volunteer basis, and most of them receive only limited travelling expenses.
Each committee works through a four-phase program: investigation, planning, scheduling and implementation, and each committee, after consultation with interested members of the public, prepares a timetable for implementation.
One can always improve methods of consultation, but it is not accurate to say that the timetable of implementation is imposed on the affected section of the economy.
With a few exceptions, mainly where the area was already subject to regulation, but also where the sector committee considers regulation desirable for orderly and fair treatment of all concerned, timetables are implemented by those the sectors represent.
The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was represented on many sector and steering committees to provide a consumer viewpoint, as well as to explain the statutory requirements of the laws administered by the department.
[ Translation]
I feel it is appropriate to reaffirm, as the commissioners did on their fifty-fifth meeting held in January, that the Metric Commission of Canada has always endeavoured to facilitate and promote voluntary conversion. At the first meeting of the commission on January 16, 1972, the commissioners had stated that the conversion to the metric system should be planned by volunteers and they had sent a questionnaire to every national association and provincial government asking for their co-operation.
Such planned but voluntary policy was again discussed at the meeting of the commission held in October, 1977. Some members of the textile industry had suggested the enforcement of regulations under the Weights and Measures Act to put an end to the use of the imperial system. Although the legislation of 1976 amending the statute law (Conversion to the Metric System) had legalized the enforcement of those regulations the commission reconfirmed its policy of voluntary conversion. The commission objected from the beginning against the enforcement of regulations providing dates for compulsory withdrawal at the outset and suggested that they would be used only to complete the conversion in a market which had implemented the metric system.
The policy of conversion by consensus was reconfirmed at the meeting of the commission in October, 1978, when the commission discussed a proposal put forward by some representatives of the textile and furniture industries aimed at drafting regulations to set dates for the compulsory withdrawal of imperial units. The commission agreed on the conversion dates timetable but only after the commission staff and the commissioners had made considerable efforts to get evidence that the textile market was already largely converted to the
June 10, 1980

metric system. Special meetings were even held to which persons opposed to the regulations were invited to voice their opinion.
For obvious safety reasons the provincial governments enacted laws regarding the metric conversion of traffic signs. However this decision was taken by the provincial transport ministers at a meeting held in Nova Scotia in 1973 independently of the commission. That decision of the premier was incorporated in the conversion master plan of the research sector and the highway maintenance and construction sector at the time when the Roads and Transportation Association of Canada agreed to constitute the nucleus of that sector's planning subcommittee. The plan, including its legal provisions was approved by the commission only on September 15, 1976.
When this regulation was deemed necessary, the commission took exceptional measures during the scheduling phase in order to see to it that all those concerned be consulted and a consensus reached.
Mr. Speaker, 1 think it will be readily recognized that this was the case with the working group on scales in the retail food industry, when volunteers from the Retail Council of Canada, the Canadian Federation of Retail Grocers, the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, the Quebec Food Retailers Association, the Canadian Institute of Food Distribution, the Consumers' Association of Canada as well as the scales manufacturing and repair industry co-operated with the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs over five years to prepare an orderly plan which, from the outset, required a consensus for the benefit of all before regulations were defined. The food retailing business, unanimously and with the support of the Consumers' Association of Canada, asked the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to prepare regulations under the Weights and Measures Act.
In 1977, an amendment to the weights and measures regulations was passed to enable the conversion of certain commodities, particularly goods sold "loose" at the retail level, to be regulated.
In effect, this set a timetable for the conversion of scales in retail food stores. The schedule as developed by the retail trade, the scale industry, consumer groups and governments divided the country into a number of areas and set dates for the conversion of each area. In this way it was intended that there would be a rapid conversion and, within a few weeks, all the merchants in an area would complete the transition so there would be no possibility of some merchants taking a commercial advantage by not converting. This is, of course, a way of proceeding about which there can be different views. In Australia, voluntary conversion was tried. When a number of difficulties were found with it, the Australians moved to greater regulation.
Metric System
Three pilot areas, Kamloops, British Columbia, Peterborough, Ontario and Sherbrooke, Quebec, completed conversion in August, 1979. Other areas were scheduled to start in January, 1980, but in December, 1979, the former government decided to halt the program.
There were some useful things learned from those pilot areas. One of them was that a month, which was the period allowed for conversion in Kamloops, was too short. Most people seemed to need four or five shopping experiences in order to convert easily from kilograms to pounds.
There are also different views on whether to allow dual pricing and dual measurement while people become accustomed. There are certain advantages seen by people in allowing dual pricing for ease in comparative shopping and comparative pricing. Against this there is rather a lot of experience to show that a very long phasing in process simply interferes with the process, and, while the costs of conversion are not inconsiderable, the final results are well worth it.
Just this evening I was talking to three people who claimed they had greatly increased their business as a result of the change to metric, which has facilitated their penetration of the overseas market.
While there are different views on the best way to proceed, I think I have shown that the methods taken up to now have in general been reasonable, thoughtful, careful and not unduly harsh or fast.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before beginning my remarks, 1 would like to make a comment on the statement of the minister this afternoon. He commented on the fact that the leaders of all the various political parties had agreed on metrication. 1 think he was referring back to 1970 when the white paper on metrication was presented to this House. If he has not seen the comments of Ged Baldwin, who was the one and only spokesman for our party at that time, I would refer him to Hansard for January 16, 1970.
While there was no doubt that all parties in the House agreed there was a need for metrication at some future time, there was certainly no agreement that metrication should be forced on the people of Canada. I wish to quote from page 2471 of Hansard for January 16, 1970. Ged Baldwin, the then hon. member for Peace River, said:
I agree that there must be a continuous and detailed study. We are prepared to co-operate with the government in this regard ... I would strongly urge the minister to give some thought to having the white paper he tabled today submitted either to a special or to a joint committee so that there might be a continuous study and reports from time to time to this committee by the boards the minister proposes to set up.
From that point on there was no referral to this House and no referral to a committee of any kind, but there was a forcing of the metric system on the people of Canada. It was in late 1976 or early 1977 that a debate took place in this House. It was a frustrating experience for those who took part in the debate. The debate was on Bill C-23, entitled "An act to facilitate conversion to the metric system of measurement". It was frustrating because it was the first occasion on which Parliament had an opportunity to debate conversion to the

June 10, 1980
Metric System
metric system and members were shocked to learn how far Canada had proceeded toward conversion on the basis of decisions made by the Metric Commission, a commission made up of bureaucrats appointed by order in council. This underlines the arrogance of the government in bypassing Parliament, ignoring our democratic system which provides for public debate by members of Parliament who are representatives of the people on matters which affect individuals so fundamentally, and which also provides for public input through committees.
What the government did was to set up a metric commission and say to a group of bureaucrats: Convert Canada to metric; ignore the cost; ignore the public and their feelings; ignore the inconvenience and ignore the fact that the United States, our largest trading partner, is moving to the metric system only with extreme caution. The government said to the Metric Commission: Push metric through at all costs. And this is exactly what the commission has been doing. They set up sector committees, around 100 of them according to an hon. member on the other side, and in my opinion they named to those committees people who were committed to metric, people who had preconceived ideas and who undertook to sell the metric system at all costs rather than to determine whether it was in the best interests of the sector or whether the people in the sector wanted to go metric.
The Metric Commission also "conned" the civil service in the various provinces to change their land title system. Saskatchewan is a prime example. In that province on April 20, 1976, an order in council was passed amending the regulations under the Land Titles Act and changing the land measurement system from acres to hectares. The hon. member for Hum-boldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) did not seem to understand this. He was accusing the federal government of making these changes. But the changes were made by the NDP government in Saskatchewan replacing acres with hectares. As I said, it was done by order in council and without any input from the MLAs or the ministers. When we found out about this order in council, we telephoned some of the MLAs in Saskatchewan and they could not believe that the regulations had been revised by order in council, so as to change acres into hectares in the province. So here we have a situation in which the NDP members are complaining about the metric system being imposed upon Canada by the Liberals in Ottawa while the NDP in Saskatchewan is doing exactly that.

speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the cost of metrication to the end of 1979 has been some $27.7 million with an additional million dollars for the Metric Monitor, that newspaper, that propaganda organ which is shipped out to various people around the country on a fairly regular basis. It is also estimated that a further $27 million will be spent in the next three years-the Metric Commission will be spending that amount. If hon. members look at the May 22, 1980 issue of Hansard they will find these figures laid out in detail in response to a question
showing what it has cost year by year to bring in metrication. Those figures refer to the cost of operating the Metric Commission alone.
It is interesting to recall what took place during the proceedings on Bill C-23. Members of the opposition, particularly those from western Canada, strenuously debated the changes provided in the bill-acres to hectares, bushels to tonnes-in the federal field covering the Canadian Wheat Board Act, the Western Grain Stabilization Act, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the two-price wheat system. It appeared to us that neither the government nor the Metric Commission understood the west and in particular they failed to understand the survey system which is based on the mile. I shall not go into the details of our survey system; the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre has already done that. I am suggesting that hon. members on the government side did not understand the situation in the west. They did not understand that farm machinery was built in sizes conforming to the imperial system, that it is calibrated for bushels rather than for kilograms and tonnes. It is very difficult, when one has to make three or four calculations, to be certain that in applying fertilizer, or chemicals for example, the right amount is getting to the ground.
In that debate on Bill C-23, the first time Parliament was given an opportunity to discuss metric, members of the Official Opposition pointed out to the government that farmers in western Canada along with the people there generally were opposed to the metric system. We understood the feelings of the farmers. We understood the feelings of those people because we were out there and we talked to them. We communicated with our constituents, because that was our job, and they told us what their feelings were. By contrast we found that the Liberal members from western Canada, such as there were, completely underestimated the depth of feeling on this topic among western farmers. They would not listen. And that is nothing new, because they have never listened. To me, the statement made by the then hon. member for Assiniboia, Ralph Goodale, on January 26, in the debate on C-23 was completely unbelievable. This is what he said in the House:
I want to deal with a few of the aspects of metric conversion affecting grain which may not be fully appreciated but upon the basis of which I believe this measure is not only supportable but is also in the best long-run interests of all segments of the grains industry, including producers in the prairie region. First, it should be noted that this change has a broad and virtually unanimous base of support in the farm community.
He went on to say that he had visited his constituency and that the people there were all in favour of metric. This was not so. When we got into committee on Bill C-23 representatives of various farm organizations appeared before us. Some of them were members of the sector committee but most of them were either paid employees or executives of the farm organizations and they said the same thing Ralph Goodale, the member from Assiniboia, was saying-that all their members were in favour of the metric system. Nevertheless, at that point in time the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), myself and others were getting petitions from the locals of the various farm organizations opposing metrication.
June 10, 1980

Those petitions and those motions were passed over to the government so that it could understand the opposition to metrication in the west. But the government paid no attention whatsoever.
Then the minister responsible at the time tried to convince us that converting bushels to tonnes and acres to hectares would mean a saving of $1 million to the grain producers of western Canada. He was never able to explain this in committee, because there was no proof that such a saving could ever be realized.
As a matter of fact, there was no saving. It was going to cost the farmers of western Canada many millions of dollars to convert to metric.
I see that my time is almost up. As far as Bill C-23 is concerned, when we found we could not convince the government to make any change, we suggested to the government that it bring in an amendment to allow a dual system; to allow the metric system and the old imperial system to operate side by side.
This, Mr. Speaker, was turned down by the then Liberal government. Fortunately, when the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Mazankowski) became the minister of transport and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, he insisted that the Canadian Wheat Board and the grain commission report using the dual system in order that those young people who understood the metric system could make use of it and the older people who understood the imperial system could make use of that. This is a sensible approach, Mr. Speaker. This is an approach this government has refused to take because they say it is voluntary.
Any time you are forced to do something by legislation it is not voluntary, it is a taking away an individual's democratic rights. This is what that government did in bringing in metrication. It brought in, in effect, legislation requiring the people of Canada to do certain things which they did not want to do, and it was brought in without any debate in this House of Commons except for Bill C-23. This is a disgrace and a sad commentary on the way the government across the way operates today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my comments this evening by saying that in spite of the caricatures which are often used in respect of debates about the metric system, it is important to take the debate about the metric system seriously, and I hope to be able to reflect a bit with hon. members this evening about just why we ought to take it seriously. It is not just a question of dinosaurs versus progressives, although indeed we have had many dinosaurs speak against metrication this evening. Here is another case of the Conservatives being right in some respects but for the wrong reasons, where they have a sort of half decent instinct, but it only manifests itself in inarticulate groanings.
Metric System
I would like, if I could, to articulate some of the resistance to the metric system this evening. Basically, the resistance is there because it is a basic conceptual change from a human system of measurement to a rationalized system; from a measurement system related to the human body to an abstract creation. The difference in how we perceive this question crosses party lines and crosses idealogical lines. I think it is important to acknowledge that. And it cannot be explained away in terms of generation gaps either. I recall, in my first election campaign that I got the most enthusiastic response ever from a group of junior high school students when I said something critical of the metric system.
So the resistance we have to the metric system is not something that is a generational thing; it is something which is very much imbedded in the way people perceive reality and I think we should acknowledge that.
Now, in addition to this conceptual change, which stirs up resistance to the system I think we need to say it has been resisted because it is a change which is seen, and rightly so, to have been imposed upon the public without adequate political debate, without adequate debate in Parliament and without adequate public debate about whether, in fact, this was something that we wanted to do. There was no consensus. From a democratic socialist point of view, Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious thing because the metric system is partly responsible for people having a very negative view of government, and in the view of our party it is very important that people have a positive view of government. We regret that the metric system has been imposed in the way that it has, because it has helped to create a negative view of government.
Human health, I believe-and I mean this in the broad sense of the health of the community-depends on people having a feeling that they are actively and creatively participating in their own reality. Robbing people of this feeling through these false bureaucratic and technocratic imperatives is very dangerous. Humans, I submit are created in the image of an active and creative God, and they will, therefore, quite appropriately resist any attempt to violate their nature in this way, whether their control over their own lives is threatened by a bureaucratic initiative, whether it is threatened by multinational corporations-no matter who happens to threaten control over their own lives.
What we have here is an example, Mr. Speaker, of how too many things are outside the pale of political debate in this country, and of how our consciousness of those things which we perceive to require political debate is too narrow. The metric system is perceived as some sort of a value neutral evolutionary imperative that really does not deserve to be talked about in any sort of political or public way.
I must give credit where credit is due, as I mentioned at the beginning when 1 referred to the Conservatives as dinosaurs. They acknowledged that some of these questions needed to be reopened, when they were in government, by suggesting a parliamentary inquiry into another issue which has proceeded in the same way as metrication, and that is the development of nuclear power in this country as if it were just part of the

June 10, 1980
Metric System
natural course of events and did not have anything to do with conscious public discussion, with opponents being made out to be members of the flat earth society.
I think in this area, as in others, Mr. Speaker, we need to expand the parameters of political debate in this country so that more and more of what we decide to do as a nation, whether we disagree with each other or not, will come within the parameters of political debate. This would be a very healthy thing, but what we are talking about here tonight is an example of just the contrary.
1 would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, not to point out, as a final reflection on this issue, the economic side of things. I say "reflection", because 1 see this debate as an opportunity to debate, really in retrospect, what has already happened. There may be some debate about the scheduling of things. There may be ways that we can talk about how we want to, and what is the best way to implement the final stages of metrication. But in a sense we are really reflecting on something that is already taking place, whether we like it or not. We have to see it as an opportunity to learn, therefore, about what kinds of mistakes not to make in the future.
As I said, 1 wanted to talk about the economic side. The Liberal government has, as usual, acted in a way that is supposedly-at least if you listen to the rhetoric-in the interests of the Canadian public but, in fact, they have acted in a way that is actually extremely insensitive to the needs of farmers, insensitive to the needs of small businessmen and insensitive to the needs of workers who never asked for metrication in the first place. But it is something which fits, as usual, perfectly into the global profit strategies of multinational corporations. It fits perfectly into the profit strategies of these global corporations, in their kingdom building aspirations, in whose long-term interests it is to create the standardization and uniformity that will result from metrication, not to mention the short-term profits they receive from smaller units for higher prices.
Global profit strategies, Mr. Speaker, by definition, require increasingly homogeneous markets and a built-in disrespect for local and traditional customs and values. My friends on the right here, who are so fond of defending these sorts of things, ought to contemplate that reality the next time they get up to defend their multinational friends. Unfortunately for the multinationals, Mr. Speaker, the human spirit, it appears to me, will prevail against all efforts to destroy our particularity and the ways in which we express ourselves in differentiated ways as human beings. Our humanity will thus prevail. This will be true of all efforts to reduce us to passive receivers of our reality and to unconscious consumers of metric hamburgers.
May we learn therefore, from the arrogance and the disembodied intellectual approach, which has characterized metrication, a new respect for the dangers of trying to change reality by undemocratic means in a democratic society.

The second point I should like to make is that I find it quite ironic the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) is the member who brought this motion before the House. On November 14, 1979, when that member was the minister of state for small businesses and industry, he said in response to a question of the hon. member for Ottawa-Carle-ton (Mr. Pepin):

The hon. member for Capilano seems to have changed his tune.
It is apparent to me that the issue of metric conversion has become an emotional issue. To get some perspective on this problem, let us look at the facts and the history of metrication. The Weights and Measures Act of 1871 established the metric system for legal use. The Canadian government policy that metric conversion was inevitable and in the national interest was established by the House leaders of all parties. On Janu-
Metric System
ary 16, 1970, the House leaders from all parties supported the white paper on metric conversion in Canada.
It is well worth noting that the white paper resulted in a response by the Canadian government to representations from diverse segments of the nation, an example of democracy in action. These representations came from groups which include the Consumers' Association of Canada, the Canadian Home and School Association, the Agricultural Institute of Canada, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association and the Canadian Council of Professional Engineers. Does the opposition party say that all those people have no relevance?

These learned groups, after great consideration, were convinced of the practical benefits to be derived from a system with advantages that range from simplifying the learning process in school to improving and consolidating Canada's position in world trade.
We should also keep in mind the voluntary nature of metric conversion. There are some 102 voluntary sector committees with over 2,000 volunteer representatives from industry, labour, consumer, and governmental bodies. Metric Commission Canada has had the over-all strategy of involving every sector from every region of Canada as soon as possible in planning for metric conversion. Sector plans are developed through a consensus process. These groups take the responsibility for monitoring the implementation of their plans. Thus, the voluntary participation approach is characterized by plans which are developed by those who will have to implement them.
After consulting with industry, labour and consumer groups, a program of guideline dates for metric conversion, recommended by Metric Commission Canada, was approved by the Canadian government and debated in the House of Commons on March 17, 1975, contrary to what the opposition has said. The Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, an all party committee, studied this matter at length and voted unanimously in favour of it. It reported back to the House on December 17, 1976, with the recommendation that the House consider the advisability of adopting this program and also of introducing additional legislation for metric conversion.
Subsequently, the Metric Conversion (Statute Law Amendment, 1976) Act was passed by the House of Commons on July 25, 1977. This was debated in the House over a period of nine months. It gave the governor in council the power to set dates in any sector of the economy, after which the customary imperial system would be illegal. Out of a total of 33 sectors which have published metric conversion plans, there are only three sectors for which regulations have been issued under the Weights and Measures Act. These regulations establish cut-off dates for the sale and advertising of goods in other than the metric system.

The moves to make metric conversion mandatory in these three sectors were therefore initiated by the industries concerned, and not by Metric Commission Canada. The regulatory action that was requested was to bring about an orderly conversion without unfair competition, reducing the possibility of consumer confusion to a minimum.
As I stated before, the House leaders of all parties spoke in 1970 in favour of the policy for metric conversion. They stated it was inevitable and in the national interest. The white paper was quite specific about some of the economic advantages of conversion.

The view is held in certain sectors of industry that Canada should not attempt conversion independently of the United States. The Canadian automobile industry, with its close ties with the United States involving common designs, production and the marketing programs, is cited as an illustration.
It appears generally the practice of the larger automobile companies to design in the measurement system of the different countries in which they manufacture. Metric or non-metric design may be translated and adapted as occasion demands. That was the situation in 1970. Today, some Canadians have a misconception about metric conversion in the United States which, of course, is our major partner.
In early 1980, a statement by President Carter in the report of the U.S. metric board to Congress reaffirmed the U.S. federal government's support for metric conversion. The United States passed a metric conversion act in 1975. With confirmation by the Senate of the United States metric board in March, 1978, and the steady conversion of United States industry and services to metric, all of Canada's trading partners either operate in metric units or are converting to them.
It is true that about 70 per cent of our exports go to the United States. The automobile and parts related manufacturing sector in the United States is leading metric conversion in North America. Over 70 per cent of manufacturing and orders for parts are already in metric units. The General Motors X-Model, 1980 cars are now 90 per cent metric, and they have stated publicly that they intend to complete the conversion of their operations by 1982.
These developments are significant for employment and production levels in over 200 companies with over 100,000 employees in southern and central Ontario and southwestern Quebec. Thirty one per cent of Canada's 1978 exports to the United States were in motor vehicles and parts. This is our biggest single manufactured export to the United States, and it amounted to over $11 billion in 1978.
Canada's third largest export to the United States is newsprint, and the exports in that industry in 1978 amounted to S2.3 billion. The paper mills in Canada have virtually completed implementation of their metric conversion plans. Even in the U.S.A., over 80 per cent of the mills label, ship and invoice using metric units.
A number of sectors in the United States are ahead of counterpart sectors in Canada. For example, Canada exports distilled liquor products to the United States and, by U.S. law, the federal alchohol U.S. administration act, all packages of spirits have been in metric units since January, 1980. At this time Canada has not converted this sector to the metric system. In addition, all new wine packaging and retailing in the United States by the same law has been in metric units since January, 1979.
1 could go on with the various examples of where Canada is behind the U.S. in metric conversion and the importance that we continue on with the metric system. I am also aware of the problems that any new change brings to the population, particularly in the stressful society in which we live today. I am concerned about the stress that relates to the elderly, but with help and understanding from the younger segments of our society the painful transition can be made, and it must be made sometime.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise to speak to the motion put forward by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) concerning the metric conversion program. 1 would like to make three points tonight on this topic. One concerns my personal experience with metric conversion, another concerns my educational experience, and finally I would like to point out the number of companies and sectors of the economy which benefit from metric conversion.
First let me share my personal experience. Ten years ago I had the opportunity to live in a country that was totally metric. I had my whole family with me including my two sons who were then aged eight and nine. They attended grades three and four in school, and in one year this eight and nine-year-old learned the metric system completely. If my children at those ages could learn the metric system in one year, then surely to goodness hon. members opposite can learn the metric conversion in their lifetimes.

I would like to share with hon. members opposite and with all hon. members of this House the Conservative government's policy for Ontario on metrication. I want to emphasize this; this is the metrication policy of the Conservative government of Ontario. As a principal of a school, I received a directive which I had to implement in my elementary school. First, all schools in the province of Ontario were told that the metric system was to become the principal system of measurement in the curriculum of the elementary and secondary schools of the province.
As 1 said, this is a directive which came from the Conservative government to every school in Ontario. Second, the metric conversion being implemented in the schools was with the

Fourth, the units and symbols of the metric system taught in the schools conform to those of the international system of units known as System International, SI, something which the hon. member who introduced the bill a couple of weeks ago was knocking down, yet this was recommended by the Conservative government of Ontario.
Fifth, metric conversion should be accepted as an opportunity to reassess pedagogical approaches towards the topic of measurement as a whole, that students be provided with opportunities to acquire a practical experimental knowledge of metric units through activity that involves comparing, estimating, measuring and related problem-solving and that teachers and students be encouraged to design and construct appropriate measuring devices to be used in conjunction with selected commercial equipment.

Mr. Speaker, this is a very important issue to all Canadians. It affects us all whether we like it or not. We all have to deal with physical things and live in the real world. When we talk about what affects the way we measure and what is in the real world, it makes us realize that metrication has an effect on us all. There are a couple of points I want to make. Time is fast disappearing.
It has been a great mistake to talk about bringing in metrication. It was pointed out many limes this afternoon and this evening that metric was made legal for purposes of trade in this country in 1871. Since that time we have had a dual system in this country in many respects.
As a cattleman, I have always talked about this. People in the medical business have always talked about cubic centimetres. That is a metric system of measure. We have alw'ays talked about kilowatts in terms of thousands or tens. When we sell our grain internationally we have people in the terminals
that export the grains acting as arbitrators; employees of the Canadian Grains Commission. They are independent. They have always weighed our grain in metric measure. Therefore, what we have is a system of duality.
We are outlawing an imperial measuring system. That is very sad. It is almost like outlawing an old friend. It is a system of measure that has served this country extremely well. As was pointed out previously, we have a system of surveying, particularly in western Canada, second to none in the world. That system has served us very well.
I find it extremely sad that we should now be bringing in something by order in council, outlawing a system of measures and weights that has served us very well. This is extremely sad.
The hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) was castigating us for not being able to learn as quickly as his children, but I challenge the hon. member to go to a service station and tell us how much air he gets in his tires measured in kilopascals. Today I phoned the Metric Commission to ask what is a kilopascal. I would like to read it into the record. It is very interesting. A pascal is the pressure or stress which is produced when the force of one newton is applied to the area of one square metre.
I must confess when I heard the word "newton" I thought they said neuter. I am in the cattle business and neuter means a certain thing to me. I am sure there are a lot of people in this country who would like to see some of those people neutered who are pushing this metric business.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

We go further. In answering the question "What is a pascal?" we end up having to ask the question, what is a newton? Well, a newton is defined as the force which, when applied to a body having a mass of one kilogram, gives the body an acceleration of one metre per second squared. When we talk about pounds per square inch we talk about weight and a system of area, which is pounds per square inch. But we are converting to kilopascals.
Look at the situation around the world. Most of the countries which have gone metric are using a system which involves millibars. It makes no sense to me that we should begin to talk about kilopascals. Back in February I went to an airport and talked to a man there who collects the data from the weather station. I asked him: Why kilopascals? He said: 1 really don't know. I read it in millibars and then convert to kilopasca's. To my mind, that makes absolutely no sense. It seems to me that when we change we should change to something that makes sense. In this case, a kilopascal means nothing. I am sure the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park would have a difficult time reading back to me or remembering what I said when I defined a kilopascal. Whether our children are learning it or not is not the point. My children are learning it and are going to feel comfortable with it. But because they are learning it 1 see no reason why whole generations ahead of them should

1 should also like to talk briefly about the system of measuring temperatures. We are changing to degrees Celsius-in my area we say "senseless" and we say "so many degrees senseless" because that is about how much sense it makes to us. On this scale there are 100 degrees between boiling and freezing- 100 gradations. On the Fahrenheit scale there are 180 degrees between boiling and freezing. 1 am in the vegetable business and when I store vegetables it is very important to have an accurate knowledge of the temperature at which those vegetables are kept. One degree "senseless" is almost two degrees Fahrenheit. I can stand a variation of one degree Fahrenheit but I cannot stand a one degree variation in terms of "senseless" because it could destroy a whole year's work. So in the process of conversion we have done some very foolish things and 1 urge hon. members opposite to consider some of the effects.
Even this afternoon, in committee, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was talking about 28 bushels per hectare. This made no sense at all because in western Canada we have been told we are going to keep the acres, so at least he could talk about acres. But he talks about bushels per hectare which is a cross, a hybrid idea-I could use a much more unpleasant word about it, but I won't.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AGENDA FOR THE MEETING OF FIRST MINISTERS ON THE CONSTITUTION OTTAWA, JUNE 9, 1980

speechtext:
1.	Review of developments since the Constitutional Conference of February, 1979.
2.	Principles for a new Canadian Constitution.

(a)	the subjects to be given priority consideration;

subtopic: A STATEMENT OF PRINCIPLES FOR A NEW CONSTITUTION

speechtext:
We, the people of Canada, proudly proclaim that we are and shall always be, with the help of God, a free and self-governing people.
Born of a meeting of the English and French presence on North American soil which had long been the home of our native peoples, and enriched by the contribution of millions of people from the four corners of the earth, we have chosen to create a life together which transcends the differences of blood relationships, language and religion, and willingly accept the experience of sharing our wealth and cultures, while respecting our diversity.
We have chosen to live together in one sovereign country, a true federation, conceived as a constitutional monarchy and founded on democratic principles.
Faithful to our history, and united by a common desire to give new life and strength to our federation, we are resolved to create together a new constitution which:
shall be conceived and adopted in Canada, shall reaffirm the official status of the French and English languages in Canada, and the diversity of cultures within Canadian society,
shall enshrine our fundamental freedoms, our basic civil, human and language rights, including the right to be educated in one's language, French or English, where numbers warrant, and the rights of our native peoples, and shall define the authority of Parliament and of the legislative assemblies of our several provinces.
We further declare that our Parliament and provincial legislatures, our various governments and their agencies shall have no other purpose than to strive for the happiness and fulfilment of each and all of us.

subtopic: PRIORITIES FOR NEW CANADIAN CONSTITUTION PROPOSED BY THE GOVERNMENT OF CANADA ON JUNE 9, 1980

speechtext:
The time has come for the Government of Canada and the governments of the provinces to join together in the task of drafting a new Canadian Constitution.
As it enters upon that task, the Government of Canada is dedicated to a full review of all constitutional measures now applying to our federation.
The whole task constitutes a great enterprise and will take time to achieve. Not all of it can be accomplished at once, nor can we wait until all of it is done to demonstrate to the people of Canada that tangible progress is being made.
The Government of Canada believes, therefore, that intensive work should now begin on a list of items of particular priority to the people of Canada and to governments, with the understanding that some or all of these could well become the subject of early adoption as parts of the new Canadian Constitution.
The list of proposed items is this:
A statement of principles A charter of rights, including language rights A dedication to Sharing and/or to Equalization: the reduction of regional disparities The patriation of the constitution Resource ownership and interprovincial trade Offshore resources Fisheries
Powers affecting the economy Communications, including broadcasting Family law
A new Upper Flouse, involving the provinces
The Supreme Court, for the people and for governments
The government also proposes that the leadership of the native peoples continue to be involved in the discussion of constitutional changes which directly affect the native peoples, in the context of the joint work on the item "Canada's Native Peoples and the Constitution". In addition, governments would pay special heed to representations from them on the items in the package set out above.
